subject: Cloud Computing
title: Load Balancers: Traffic Directors
description: A 60-second lesson on Load Balancers: Traffic Directors.

hook.text: A million users hit your website at once. Without help, one server drowns while others sit idle.

buildup.text: A load balancer distributes incoming requests across many servers so no single one is overwhelmed.

discovery.text: It checks server health constantly. If one fails, traffic routes to the survivors instantly.

twist.text: Modern load balancers are smart. They route by geography, content type, or even user identity.

climax.text: Every major website you use sits behind a load balancer. You just never see it working.

punchline.text: Load balancers keep sites alive. Invisibly.

quiz.question: What is the primary role of a load balancer?
options: Distributing incoming traffic across multiple servers to prevent overload
Compressing data to reduce bandwidth costs
Encrypting all traffic between users and servers

details.summary: Load balancers distribute incoming traffic across multiple servers to prevent any single server from becoming overwhelmed. They check server health, route traffic intelligently, handle SSL termination, and automatically adjust as servers are added or removed through auto-scaling.
details.whyItMatters: Load balancers are essential for running reliable, scalable applications in the cloud. They allow horizontal scaling and ensure traffic goes only to healthy servers.
takeaways: Load balancers distribute traffic across multiple servers
Health checks route traffic only to healthy instances
They enable horizontal scaling without application changes

faq.question: What types of load balancers exist?
faq.answer: Layer 4 load balancers route based on IP and port, operating at the transport level. Layer 7 load balancers inspect HTTP content and can route based on URL paths, headers, or cookies. Cloud providers offer both types, with Layer 7 being more common for web applications.

faq.question: How do load balancers check server health?
faq.answer: Load balancers periodically send health check requests to each server. If a server fails consecutive checks, the load balancer stops sending traffic to it. When the server passes checks again, it is gradually brought back into rotation. This happens automatically.
